references.text: The preceding verse in Luke describes the persecution believers will experience and forms the context for the call to rejoice in verse 23.

The parallel passage in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says, 'Rejoice and be glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.' Almost identical content.
The apostles left the council rejoicing because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus—an example of rejoicing under persecution.
Stephen asks, 'Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?' This confirms Jesus' words that their fathers persecuted the prophets.
Peter encourages believers to rejoice when they share in Christ's sufferings, because the glory of God's Spirit rests upon them—the same theme of joy amid persecution.
James urges believers to consider it pure joy when they face various trials—joy in the midst of adversity.
The people of Israel mocked God's messengers, despised his words and scoffed at the prophets—an example of how their fathers persecuted the prophets.
Nehemiah describes how the people of Israel were disobedient and killed the prophets who testified against them—a confirmation of the persecution of the prophets.
The prophet Uriah prophesied against Jerusalem and was pursued and killed by King Jehoiakim—a concrete example of how their fathers persecuted the prophets.
Elijah complains that the people of Israel have abandoned the covenant, torn down the altars and killed the prophets—their fathers persecuted the prophets.
Jesus laments over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those sent to the city—the persecution of God's messengers throughout history.
The listing in Hebrews of heroes of faith who were persecuted, mocked, flogged, imprisoned and killed—examples of prophets and believers who suffered for their faith.

Paul writes that we suffer with Christ so that we may also be glorified with him, and that present sufferings cannot compare with the glory to be revealed—the reward in heaven outweighs the suffering.
Paul describes the current trouble as light and momentary, working out an eternal weight of glory—a parallel to the great reward in heaven.
The blessing on those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for the kingdom of heaven is theirs—the context for the promise of a great reward in heaven.
